publications.name: Saving as a Luxury Good: Why Progressive Taxation Cannot Guarantee Falling Inequality
publications.summary: Saving as a Luxury Good: Why Progressive Taxation Cannot Guarantee Falling Inequality. When the rich save a larger share of their wealth, no progressive tax guarantees that inequality falls over time. We show the classical characterizations hold within a period but not across periods, and that what governs the trajectory is a schedule's residual progression, a parameter every enacted and proposed wealth tax leaves untouched.

publications.name: The Myth of the Informed Voter
publications.summary: The Myth of the Informed Voter. Even fully informed voters can be decided by which issues a campaign makes salient rather than by what they know: money shapes elections through attention, not information. A binding spending cap forces competition across many issues at once, though whether it seats the broadly representative candidate depends on the structure of the electorate.

publications.name: Saving as Instrument and Status: Progressive Taxation in a Dynamic Economy
publications.summary: Saving as Instrument and Status: Progressive Taxation in a Dynamic Economy. Extends my job market paper to forward-looking agents, testing whether its non-convergence result depends on myopia. It does not. Anticipating the returns to accumulation, the wealthy save more aggressively still, and containing the divergence requires marginal-rate progressivity, a stricter standard than average-rate.
